content.text:
## Summary

I was not able to identify a single, specific, publicly available medical‑necessity policy document that this payer applied to Jordan Jennings's CPT 22612 request, because **the notice does not identify which entity actually made the medical‑necessity decision.**

"Medicaid, state of Texas" is not itself a payer — Texas Medicaid operates through:
- **Fee‑for‑service Texas Medicaid**, administered by Texas Medicaid & Healthcare Partnership (TMHP), whose prior‑authorization rules are published in the *Texas Medicaid Provider Procedures Manual (TMPPM)*; or
- One of several **STAR/STAR+PLUS managed‑care organizations (MCOs)** — e.g., Aetna, Molina Healthcare, Superior HealthPlan, UnitedHealthcare Community Plan, Wellpoint (formerly Amerigroup), Community Health Choice, Cook Children's Health Plan, Driscoll Health Plan, El Paso Health, Community First — each of which maintains its **own** internal clinical/medical policy for lumbar spinal fusion (e.g., UnitedHealthcare Community Plan has a "Spinal Fusion and Decompression" policy; other MCOs have comparable but distinct documents, often built on InterQual or MCG criteria plus company-specific overlays).

Because the denial letter does not state which MCO (or TMHP fee-for-service) issued it, I cannot truthfully name "the" governing policy — doing so would be guessing among several plausible but different documents, each with different criteria, numbers, and effective dates. I did confirm real candidate documents exist (e.g., a UnitedHealthcare Community Plan "Spinal Fusion and Decompression" clinical policy, and TMHP's TMPPM prior-authorization chapter), but without confirmation of the actual plan administrator I cannot verify which one — if any — was actually applied to this member.

  "effective_date": null,

  "submission_route": "Not confirmable without knowing which entity issued the denial. In general, Texas Medicaid appeals of a medical-necessity denial go to: (1) the plan's own Member Appeals/Grievance unit first (address/fax/phone is printed on the actual denial letter and in the Member Handbook — for MCOs this is usually a P.O. box plus a toll-free member-services number; for TMHP fee-for-service it is TMHP's Prior Authorization Appeals unit), and (2) if the internal appeal is denied (or simultaneously, for Medicaid), the member also has the separate right to request a Texas Health and Human Services Commission (HHSC) State Fair Hearing. The reference number POC-7B726A30C1-53854 and the phone number/address on the original letter (not shown in the excerpt provided) are the correct first point of contact — the patient should call that number to confirm the payer's identity and appeal mailing address/fax/portal.",
  "how_to_obtain_criteria": "Because U.S. and Texas Medicaid managed-care rules (Title 42 CFR §438.404 and Texas Insurance Code/HHSC managed-care contract requirements) entitle a member to the specific medical necessity criteria, clinical guideline, or medical policy relied upon in a denial, the patient (or their provider) should: (1) Call the Member Services number printed on the denial letter or on the back of the Medicaid ID card to identify which entity issued the denial — TMHP fee-for-service or a named STAR/STAR+PLUS MCO (Aetna, Molina, Superior HealthPlan, UnitedHealthcare Community Plan, Wellpoint, Community Health Choice, Cook Children's, Driscoll, Community First, or El Paso Health). (2) Explicitly request, in writing, 'a copy of the specific medical policy, clinical criteria, or guideline used to deny CPT 22612,' which the plan is required to provide under Medicaid managed-care transparency rules. (3) If it is a managed-care denial, also request the plan's 'Clinical Policy' or 'Medical Policy' library reference number cited in the denial letter/ Notice of Adverse Benefit Determination — federal Medicaid rules (42 CFR 438.404(b)) require the notice to identify the specific rule, standard, or criteria that was the basis for the decision; if this notice as given to the patient omits that citation, that omission itself can be raised as a procedural defect in the appeal. (4) Separately, request a State Fair Hearing packet from HHSC, which includes the right to review the full case file, including the criteria applied, before or at the hearing.",
  "confidence": "low",
  "notes": "I deliberately did not name a specific policy (e.g., a particular MCO's 'Spinal Fusion and Decompression' policy or the TMHP TMPPM surgery chapter) as 'the' governing document, because the denial letter you provided does not state which Medicaid entity (TMHP fee-for-service vs. a specific STAR/STAR+PLUS MCO) issued it, and different entities apply materially different criteria. Naming one without confirmation would risk giving you the wrong appeal target and the wrong clinical criteria to rebut. Please obtain the plan/administrator name (from the ID card, EOB, or by calling the number on the denial letter) and I can then locate and quote the exact applicable medical policy and its lumbar-fusion medical-necessity criteria (which for essentially all payers in this space typically require, in some combination: a confirmed structural diagnosis such as spondylolisthesis, instability, or degenerative disc disease correlating with imaging; failure of at least 6 months of conservative/nonoperative treatment such as physical therapy, medication, and/or epidural injections; absence of significant contraindicating comorbidities/psychosocial factors; and correlation of symptoms with imaging findings at the level to be fused). Also note the 180-day appeal window stated in your letter is unusually long for Texas Medicaid managed care (which typically requires internal appeal within 60 days of the denial notice, with a further window to request an HHSC State Fair Hearing) — confirm this date is correct by checking the full original notice and Member Handbook before relying on it, since missing the true, shorter deadline could forfeit appeal rights even if this summary's date has not yet passed."
}

**Bottom line:** I could not verify a specific, applicable medical policy document because the denial letter itself does not disclose which Texas Medicaid entity (TMHP fee-for-service or which specific STAR/STAR+PLUS MCO) made this determination — and Texas Medicaid managed-care organizations each publish distinct spinal-fusion medical-necessity policies. The single most useful next step is for the patient/provider to call the number on the actual denial letter, confirm the issuing entity, and demand (in writing) the specific medical policy or clinical criteria cited as the basis for denial — which federal Medicaid regulations require the plan to disclose.
